pos: n. (a mother's or father's mother; in 2 Timothy the first link in a chain of covenant faith, and in Kings a queen removed for idolatry)
etymology: From grand (French grand, great) and mother. The Greek in 2 Timothy 1:5 is mamme, a nursery word for grandmother; the Authorized Version's marginal notes supply the sense at 1 Kings 15:10 where the Hebrew says simply mother.
biblical_def: “When I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that in thee also” (2 Timothy 1:5). Paul names three generations and puts the grandmother first. Timothy's father was a Greek, and the household instruction came from the women: “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15). The faith is called unfeigned — unhypocritical, the same in the grandmother as in the boy. The other side of the picture is Maachah, grandmother of Asa. The Authorized Version's margin at 1 Kings 15:10 notes that mother there means grandmother, and her influence was idolatrous: “And also Maachah his mother, even her he removed from being queen, because she had made an idol in a grove; and Asa destroyed her idol, and burnt it by the brook Kidron” (1 Kings 15:13). A grandmother in Scripture is therefore never a decorative figure. She is a channel, and what passes through her passes to the third generation either way.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grandmother as the mother of one's father or mother, and grandchild as the son or daughter of one's son or daughter.
webster_full: GRANDMOTHER, n. The mother of one's father or mother.
GRANDCHILD, n. A son's or daughter's child; a child in the second degree of descent.
UNFEIGNED, a. Not feigned; not counterfeit; not hypocritical; real; sincere.
POSTERITY, n. Descendants; children, children's children, &c. indefinitely.
NURTURE, n. That which nourishes; education; instruction.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 1:5
When I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that in thee also.
2 Timothy 3:15
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
1 Kings 15:13
And also Maachah his mother, even her he removed from being queen, because she had made an idol in a grove; and Asa destroyed her idol, and burnt it by the brook Kidron.
2 Chronicles 15:16

And also concerning Maachah the mother of Asa the king, he removed her from being queen, because she had made an idol in a grove: and Asa cut down her idol, and stamped it, and burnt it at the brook Kidron.
corruption_summary: Discipleship is imagined as a programme run by professionals, and the household chain Paul actually names is treated as sentiment.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul is writing to a minister he calls his own son in the faith, and when he accounts for that man's faith he names two women and a childhood spent in the Scriptures. No church programme appears in the sentence. The modern arrangement outsources the formation of children to age-segregated ministries staffed by the young, and grandparents are given a role in the family and almost none in its instruction. Deuteronomy 4:9 commands the opposite explicitly — teach them thy sons, and thy sons' sons — and 2 Timothy 1:5 records what happens when it is obeyed. The chain of covenant instruction is generational by design, and the middle link is not the church staff.

Maachah is the necessary warning against sentimentalising the point. A grandmother is a channel, and Asa found the idol at the top of his own household and had to burn it by the brook Kidron and remove his own grandmother from being queen. That is one of the hardest acts of reform recorded of any king of Judah, and it is commended. Honour for the aged is commanded in the same Scriptures that record it, and neither cancels the other: a family may owe deep respect to a forebear and still be obliged to cut down what she planted. Households pass on what they have, and what they have is not always faith.
roots_summary: Greek mamme (G3125), grandmother — 2 Timothy 1:5, its only occurrence; anupokritos (G505), unfeigned — same verse; Hebrew em, mother, used of a grandmother at 1 Kings 15:10.
roots_lines: Greek mamme (G3125) — grandmother; 2 Timothy 1:5, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Greek anupokritos (G505) — unfeigned, without hypocrisy; 2 Timothy 1:5, and of love in Romans 12:9.
Greek enoikeo (G1774) — to dwell in; 2 Timothy 1:5, the faith dwelt first in Lois.
Hebrew em — mother; used at 1 Kings 15:10 and 2 Chronicles 15:16 of Maachah, whom the margin identifies as Asa's grandmother.
Deuteronomy 4:9 gives the standing command: teach them thy sons, and thy sons' sons.
usage: “Which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois” — the chain begins two generations back.
“From a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” — the curriculum of that household.
Asa removed his own grandmother from being queen and burnt her idol.

pos: n. (the conceiving of a child; in Scripture an act attributed to the LORD, and a point at which sin is already present)
etymology: Latin conceptio, from concipere, to take together, to conceive. The Hebrew rendered conception is generally heron or herayon, from harah, to conceive.
biblical_def: The word first appears in the sentence on the woman: “Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee” (Genesis 3:16). Childbearing is not itself the curse — it was commanded before the fall — but it is brought under sorrow. The second use is one of the tenderest sentences in the historical books: “So Boaz took Ruth, and she was his wife: and when he went in unto her, the LORD gave her conception, and she bare a son” (Ruth 4:13). Conception is given, and the Giver is named; the son born is the grandfather of David. Hosea pronounces the reverse as a judgment: “As for Ephraim, their glory shall fly away like a bird, from the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception” (Hosea 9:11) — barrenness at three stages, and each stage assumes a life God was withholding. David locates his own sinfulness at the same point: “Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psalm 51:5). Whatever else that verse teaches, it assumes there was a me to be conceived in sin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conception as the act of conceiving, the first formation of the embryo of an animal, and also the act of the mind in forming an idea.
webster_full: CONCEPTION, n. The act of conceiving; the first formation of the embryo or fetus of an animal.
2. The state of being conceived.
3. In pneumatology, apprehension of any thing by the mind; the act of conceiving in the mind.
CONCEIVE, v.t. To receive into the womb and breed; to begin the formation of the embryo.
BARREN, a. Not producing young; not prolific.
scriptures: Ruth 4:13
So Boaz took Ruth, and she was his wife: and when he went in unto her, the LORD gave her conception, and she bare a son.
Genesis 3:16
Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.
Psalm 51:5
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
Hosea 9:11
As for Ephraim, their glory shall fly away like a bird, from the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception.
corruption_summary: The beginning of a life is made a question of definition to be settled by convenience, and Scripture treats it as a gift with an Author.
corruption_paragraphs: Ruth 4:13 states the biblical account of the matter in six words: the LORD gave her conception. Conception is not primarily a biological event that may or may not be assigned personal status by a legislature; it is a gift, and the Giver is God. Psalm 51:5 assumes a self already present and already fallen at that point, and Psalm 139 describes the same person being covered in his mother's womb and written in God's book when as yet there was none of them. Whatever difficulty attends the hardest cases — and they are genuinely hard, and deserve compassion rather than slogans — the framework in which a life at its beginning is a matter of definition rather than of gift is not one Scripture supplies.

The second corruption runs the other way and is found among people who hold the right doctrine. Genesis 3:16 places conception and childbearing under sorrow, and Hosea shows barrenness pronounced as judgment; both texts take for granted that this is an area of real grief. Churches which speak of children only as blessing, and never of the wombs God has shut, leave the barren woman without a word. Hannah, Sarah, Rachel, Rebekah and Elisabeth are all in the record, and the God who gave Ruth conception is the same God who withheld it from them for years. The doctrine is not that children always come, but that they are always given.
roots_summary: Hebrew harah, to conceive, and the nouns heron and herayon — Genesis 3:16, Ruth 4:13, Hosea 9:11; Greek sullambano (G4815), to conceive — Luke 1:24, 1:31.
roots_lines: Hebrew harah — to conceive, to be with child; the root behind every Old Testament occurrence.
Hebrew herayon — conception; Genesis 3:16, brought under sorrow in the sentence on the woman.
Hebrew nathan — to give; Ruth 4:13, the LORD gave her conception.
Greek sullambano (G4815) — to conceive; Luke 1:24 of Elisabeth and Luke 1:31 of the virgin.
Psalm 139:16 states the corresponding doctrine: thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect.
usage: “The LORD gave her conception” — a gift, with a named Giver.
“In sin did my mother conceive me” — there was a me to be conceived.
“From the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception” — three stages, and each a withholding.

pos: n. (a woman of royal rank; the meaning of Sarah's new name, and the title Jerusalem lost)
etymology: From prince, Latin princeps, first, with the feminine ending. The Hebrew sarah means princess, from sar, a prince or chief — which is why the Authorized Version's margin at Genesis 17:15 explains the new name.
biblical_def: The word enters Scripture as a renaming. “And God said unto Abraham, As for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be” (Genesis 17:15) — and the Authorized Version's margin notes that Sarah means princess. The reason follows: “And I will bless her, and give thee a son also of her: yea, I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations; kings of people shall be of her” (Genesis 17:16). The title is not decorative; she is renamed princess because kings will come out of her, and she is ninety years old and barren when it is given. The other great use is a lament. Jerusalem, fallen: “How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!” (Lamentations 1:1). The city is figured as a woman who held the rank and lost it. Between the two texts lies the whole logic of covenant honour: it is conferred by God on the barren and the unlikely, and it is forfeited by unfaithfulness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a princess as a female sovereign, the daughter of a king, or the consort of a prince.
webster_full: PRINCESS, n. A female sovereign, as an empress or queen.
2. A sovereign lady of rank next to that of a queen.
3. The daughter of a king.
4. The consort of a prince; as the princess of Wales.
TRIBUTARY, a. Paying tribute to another, either from compulsion, as an acknowledgment of submission, or to secure protection.
scriptures: Genesis 17:15
And God said unto Abraham, As for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be.
Genesis 17:16
And I will bless her, and give thee a son also of her: yea, I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations; kings of people shall be of her.
Lamentations 1:1
How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!
1 Kings 11:3
And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart.
corruption_summary: The word has been captured by a marketing register that offers girls a title without a covenant, and Scripture attaches it to promise and to loss.
corruption_paragraphs: The princess of contemporary children's culture is an identity conferred by feeling and consumption: a girl is told she is a princess as an affirmation, and the title carries no lineage, no duty and no risk. Sarah's title came with a promise she laughed at and a body that could not fulfil it, and it obliged her to believe God for twenty-five years. Lamentations shows the other end — a princess among the provinces reduced to tributary widowhood by her own unfaithfulness. Honour in Scripture is always conferred within a covenant, and what is conferred within a covenant can be forfeited. That is a harder and better thing to tell a daughter than that she is a princess because she is herself.

Solomon's seven hundred wives, princesses (1 Kings 11:3) is the reminder that the rank guarantees nothing. Those women were royalty, and the sentence that follows is and his wives turned away his heart. Rank in the Bible is real, and it is never the thing that matters most about a person; Ruth the Moabitess enters the same royal line by faith and loyalty with no title at all. The dictionary's standard elsewhere applies here: the creational order gives men and women distinct callings of genuine dignity, and neither is dignified by flattery.
roots_summary: Hebrew sarah, princess — the name given at Genesis 17:15; sar, a prince or chief; sarah in the plural for Solomon's royal wives, 1 Kings 11:3; sarati, princess among the provinces — Lamentations 1:1.
roots_lines: Hebrew sarah — princess; the name God gives Abraham's wife at Genesis 17:15, explained in the Authorized Version's margin.
Hebrew sar — a prince, chief, captain; the masculine root of the name.
Hebrew sarah plural — princesses; 1 Kings 11:3, of Solomon's royal wives who turned away his heart.
Hebrew Sarai — the earlier form of the name, changed at the giving of the covenant sign.
Hebrews 11:11 records the outcome: through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive seed.
usage: “But Sarah shall her name be” — princess, given to a barren woman of ninety.
“Princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!” — the rank can be lost.
“Seven hundred wives, princesses… and his wives turned away his heart” — rank guarantees nothing.

pos: n. (a religious festival day; in Psalm 42 remembered with longing, and in Colossians named among the shadows fulfilled in Christ)
etymology: From holy and day, and the ancestor of the modern holiday — a drift that records what happened to the institution. In Colossians 2:16 it renders Greek heorte, a feast.
biblical_def: The Psalmist, in exile from the sanctuary, remembers what he has lost: “When I remember these things, I pour out my soul in me: for I had gone with the multitude, I went with them to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise, with a multitude that kept holyday” (Psalm 42:4). What he misses is corporate — the multitude, the going with them, the voice of joy and praise — and the memory of it is what makes his present thirst so sharp. Paul uses the word in his warning against those who would bind the Colossians to the ceremonial calendar: “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days” (Colossians 2:16). The ground is given in the next verse and it is Christological, not indifferentist: these things “are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Colossians 2:17). The feasts were not empty; they were shadows cast by a body that has now arrived. A man who returns to the shadow after the body has come is not more devout, and no one may judge a believer for declining to.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines holyday as a day set apart for commemorating some important event, a religious anniversary, and notes its use for a day of joy and gaiety.
webster_full: HOLYDAY, n. A day set apart for commemorating some important event; an anniversary consecrated to religious observance.
2. A day of joy and gaiety.
3. A day of exemption from labor; a day of amusement.
FESTIVAL, n. The time of feasting; an anniversary day of joy, civil or religious.
SHADOW, n. A representation of something made by light; hence, an imperfect and faint representation, opposed to substance.
scriptures: Psalm 42:4
When I remember these things, I pour out my soul in me: for I had gone with the multitude, I went with them to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise, with a multitude that kept holyday.
Colossians 2:16
Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:
Colossians 2:17
Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.
Leviticus 23:39

Also in the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when ye have gathered in the fruit of the land, ye shall keep a feast unto the LORD seven days: on the first day shall be a sabbath, and on the eighth day shall be a sabbath.
corruption_summary: The word's own history tells the story: a holy day became a holiday, and the day off outlived the thing it was for.
corruption_paragraphs: Holyday and holiday are the same word, and the split between them is a record of what the culture did with the institution. The day was set apart for God, then set apart from work, then simply set apart for the self. Every major Christian observance in the West has completed some portion of that journey. The remedy is not the recovery of a crowded liturgical calendar, which Colossians 2:16 expressly refuses to impose; it is the recovery of the one day God has appointed for His church — the Lord's Day — as a day of worship rather than a slot of leisure. The regulative principle bears directly here: what God has commanded for corporate worship is required, and what He has not commanded may not be bound on the conscience.

Colossians 2:16 is misused in both directions. Some quote it to prove that all days are alike and therefore that no day is to be kept, which ignores that the Lord's Day is the settled practice of the New Testament church and confessed as the Christian sabbath. Others ignore it entirely and rebuild the ceremonial calendar as a mark of seriousness. Paul's argument is against neither observance nor liberty as such but against judging a brother over the shadows, since the body is of Christ. Psalm 42:4 supplies the pastoral counterweight to all such disputes: what the exile longed for was not the calendar but the multitude, the house of God, and the voice of joy and praise.
roots_summary: Greek heorte (G1859), a feast — Colossians 2:16; skia (G4639), a shadow — Colossians 2:17; Hebrew chagag, to keep festival — Psalm 42:4.
roots_lines: Greek heorte (G1859) — a festival; Colossians 2:16, and used throughout the Gospels of the Jewish feasts.
Greek skia (G4639) — a shadow; Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 8:5, Hebrews 10:1 — the shadow implies a body casting it.
Greek soma (G4983) — body, substance; Colossians 2:17, set against the shadow.
Hebrew chagag — to keep a pilgrim feast; Psalm 42:4, of the multitude that kept holyday.
Hebrews 10:1 states the same principle: the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things.
usage: “With a multitude that kept holyday” — what the exile missed was the multitude.
“Let no man therefore judge you… in respect of an holyday” — the shadow may not bind the conscience.
“The body is of Christ” — the shadows were cast by something real.

pos: n. pl. (structures; in the Olivet discourse the temple complex the disciples admired and the Lord condemned)
etymology: From build, Old English byldan, to construct a dwelling. The Greek oikodome is used both for a physical structure and, throughout Paul, for the edifying of the church — the same word builds stones and saints.
biblical_def: “And Jesus went out, and departed from the temple: and his disciples came to him for to shew him the buildings of the temple” (Matthew 24:1). Mark records the disciple's exclamation: “Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!” (Mark 13:1). Their admiration was not foolish — Herod's temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world, and it was still unfinished. The reply is the beginning of the Olivet discourse: “Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mark 13:2), and Matthew records the same sentence (Matthew 24:2). It was fulfilled within that generation, in the year 70. The lesson is not that buildings are wrong; God gave the pattern for tabernacle and temple in exact detail and filled both with His glory. It is that the most magnificent structure ever raised for the worship of the true God was, at that moment, under sentence, because the One it was built to point to was walking out of it. The stones the disciples admired had already outlived their purpose.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a building as a fabric or edifice constructed for use or convenience, and building as the art of constructing edifices.
webster_full: BUILDING, n. A fabric or edifice constructed for use or convenience, as a house, a church, a shop.
2. The art of constructing edifices, or the practice of civil architecture.
BUILD, v.t. To frame, construct and raise, as an edifice or fabric of almost any kind.
2. To raise by art; to frame or shape into a particular form.
EDIFY, v.t. To instruct and improve the mind in knowledge generally, and particularly in moral and religious knowledge.
scriptures: Mark 13:1
And as he went out of the temple, one of his disciples saith unto him, Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!
Mark 13:2
And Jesus answering said unto him, Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
Matthew 24:1
And Jesus went out, and departed from the temple: and his disciples came to him for to shew him the buildings of the temple.
Matthew 24:2
And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
corruption_summary: A congregation identifies itself with its property, and the Lord's answer to men admiring stones is left unread.
corruption_paragraphs: The disciples pointed at the buildings, and the Lord answered by announcing their demolition. He did not say the temple was worthless; He said it was finished. That exchange is worth putting beside every congregational discussion of property, because churches routinely identify their life with a structure — naming, debt, sentiment and identity all attached to a building, so that its loss is felt as the death of the church. In the New Testament the temple is fulfilled in Christ and the building God is now raising is a people: ye are God's building, an habitation of God through the Spirit. Stones are useful and they are not the church.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the double meaning of the Greek word. Oikodome is a structure and it is also the edifying of the saints, and the New Testament spends far more effort on the second than the first. Paul's test for what happens in an assembly is whether it builds up; the buildings that concerned him were people. A church that can say precisely what its facility cost, and could not say who in it has been built up in the last year, has kept the disciples' question and missed the Lord's answer.
roots_summary: Greek oikodome (G3619), a building and also edification — Matthew 24:1, Mark 13:1-2, 1 Corinthians 3:9, Ephesians 4:12.
roots_lines: Greek oikodome (G3619) — a building; Matthew 24:1 and Mark 13:1-2 of the temple, and Ephesians 4:12 of the edifying of the body of Christ.
Greek oikodomeo (G3618) — to build; used of houses, of the church, and of the Lord's promise to build His church on the rock.
Greek lithos (G3037) — a stone; Mark 13:2, not one left upon another, and 1 Peter 2:5 of living stones.
Greek kataluo (G2647) — to throw down, to dissolve; Mark 13:2, of the buildings.
1 Corinthians 3:9 gives the New Testament substitute: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building.
usage: “See what manner of stones and what buildings are here!” — and the answer was a demolition notice.
“There shall not be left one stone upon another” — fulfilled within that generation.
The same Greek word builds stones and saints.

pos: n. (the royal or sacred vestry, and the office of its keeper; the post held by Huldah the prophetess's husband)
etymology: From Old French warderobe, a place to guard robes. The Hebrew is beged, garment, in a construction meaning keeper of the garments — a real office in the royal and temple establishment.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice, in parallel accounts of the same errand, and both times it identifies a man by his job in order to locate his wife. Josiah's men, holding a book of the law found in the temple, are sent to enquire of the LORD: “So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her” (2 Kings 22:14). Chronicles records it identically (2 Chronicles 34:22). The mission was urgent — “great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book” (2 Kings 22:13) — and Huldah's answer, delivered in the ordinary form of prophetic speech, both confirmed the coming judgment and granted Josiah a reprieve: “thine eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place” (2 Kings 22:20). The keeper of the wardrobe kept the vestments; his wife was consulted by the king's highest officers, in her own house, and the whole reformation of Judah turned on what she said.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wardrobe as a room or portable closet in which wearing apparel is kept, and also wearing apparel in general.
webster_full: WARDROBE, n. A room or apartment where clothes are kept.
2. Wearing apparel in general.
VESTRY, n. A room appendant to a church, in which the sacerdotal vestments and sacred utensils are kept.
VESTMENT, n. A garment; some part of clothing or dress; particularly, a long outer garment.
PROPHETESS, n. A female prophet.
scriptures: 2 Kings 22:14

So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her.
2 Kings 22:13

Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.
2 Kings 22:20

Behold therefore, I will gather thee unto thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace; and thine eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place. And they brought the king word again.
2 Chronicles 34:22

And Hilkiah, and they that the king had appointed, went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvath, the son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college:) and they spake to her to that effect.
corruption_summary: Huldah is enlisted to overturn the New Testament's ordering of the church, or else quietly passed over by those the ordering protects.
corruption_paragraphs: Huldah is regularly produced as proof that Scripture knows no distinction of office between men and women, since the high priest himself came to her for a word from the LORD. The argument moves too fast. Huldah gave a prophetic word in her own house to a delegation; she did not hold the priesthood, did not serve at the altar, and did not exercise rule in the assembly. The New Testament likewise records Philip's four daughters who prophesied and Anna in the temple, alongside the plain instruction that a woman is not to teach nor usurp authority over the man, grounded in the creational order of 1 Timothy 2:13. The offices of elder and deacon are the questions in dispute, and prophetic speech was never restricted the way office is.

The opposite failure belongs to churches that hold the right doctrine and then behave as though women had no part in the life of the covenant people at all. Josiah's reformation — the greatest recorded of any king of Judah — turned on the word of a woman whom the king's officers sought out by name when Jeremiah and Zephaniah were both alive. She is called the prophetess without apology, and her word is recorded as the word of the LORD. Any complementarianism that cannot say that plainly is not the Bible's, and it will keep losing daughters to the framework it refuses to answer.
roots_summary: Hebrew shomer habbegadim, keeper of the garments — 2 Kings 22:14, 2 Chronicles 34:22; nebiah, prophetess — the title given Huldah, Miriam, Deborah and Anna's counterparts.
roots_lines: Hebrew beged — a garment; in the construction rendered keeper of the wardrobe, Shallum's office.
Hebrew shamar — to keep, to guard; the verb behind the title of the office.
Hebrew nebiah — prophetess; used of Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Deborah (Judges 4:4) and Huldah (2 Kings 22:14).
Hebrew mishneh — the second quarter or district of Jerusalem, rendered the college in the Authorized Version.
2 Kings 22:16-17 records her message: the LORD will bring evil upon this place, according to all the words of the book.
usage: “Keeper of the wardrobe” — a real office in the royal establishment.
“They went unto Huldah the prophetess… and they communed with her” — the king's highest officers, at her house.
The reformation of Judah turned on what she said.

pos: n. (confinement in prison; a penalty in the Persian decree, and one of the trials endured by the faithful of Hebrews 11)
etymology: From imprison, Old French emprisoner, to put in prison. The Greek in Hebrews 11:36 is phulake, a guarding or a place of guarding, hence a prison.
biblical_def: Artaxerxes' commission to Ezra lists the penalties the returning scribe may impose: “And whosoever will not do the law of thy God, and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him, whether it be unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment” (Ezra 7:26). Four penalties, and imprisonment is the least of them — a striking arrangement to modern eyes, since ancient justice used prison chiefly to hold a man before trial rather than as the standard sentence. The other use puts imprisonment among the sufferings of the faithful: “And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment” (Hebrews 11:36). The list continues into the terrible catalogue of verse 37 — stoned, sawn asunder, slain with the sword, wandering in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, tormented — and the writer says of them all that the world was not worthy. Paul knew the thing directly and lists it among his credentials: “In stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings” (2 Corinthians 6:5). Half the New Testament epistles were written by a man under guard.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imprisonment as the act of putting in a prison, confinement in a place, and restraint of a man's personal liberty.
webster_full: IMPRISONMENT, n. The act of putting and confining in prison; the act of arresting and detaining in custody.
2. Confinement in a place; restraint of liberty.
PRISON, n. A house or place of confinement, particularly for debtors and criminals.
BONDS, n. plu. Chains; imprisonment; captivity.
BANISHMENT, n. The act of a prince or magistrate compelling a citizen to leave his own country.
scriptures: Hebrews 11:36
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:
Hebrews 11:37
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Ezra 7:26

And whosoever will not do the law of thy God, and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him, whether it be unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment.
2 Corinthians 6:5
In stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings;
corruption_summary: Hebrews 11 is preached as a gallery of victories, and the second half of the chapter — where faith is rewarded with chains — is skipped.
corruption_paragraphs: The famous chapter divides sharply at verse 35. Before it, faith stops the mouths of lions, quenches fire and turns armies to flight; after it, faith is tortured, mocked, scourged, imprisoned and sawn asunder. The writer makes no distinction in quality between the two groups — these all, having obtained a good report through faith — and the second list is longer. Preaching that treats the chapter as a catalogue of what faith achieves, and stops where the achievements stop, teaches a doctrine the chapter itself refutes. Faith is not a technique for producing deliverance. It is confidence in God that persists when deliverance does not come, and the writer says the world was not worthy of the people in the second half.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the New Testament's ordinary expectation that the faithful will be imprisoned, and the corresponding duty in the same epistle: remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them. Hebrews assumes a church that visits prisons because its own members keep ending up in them. Christians in much of the world need no instruction on this; those in comfortable places, who are far more likely to encounter the subject as a matter of policy debate than of visiting a brother, should notice that Scripture treats it as a plain and continuing obligation of the congregation.
roots_summary: Greek phulake (G5438), a prison — Hebrews 11:36, 2 Corinthians 6:5; desmos (G1199), bonds — Hebrews 11:36; Aramaic term for imprisonment in the decree of Ezra 7:26.
roots_lines: Greek phulake (G5438) — a guarding, a prison; Hebrews 11:36, 2 Corinthians 6:5, and throughout Acts.
Greek desmos (G1199) — a band, a bond; Hebrews 11:36, and Paul's frequent word for his own chains.
Greek desmios (G1198) — a prisoner; Paul's self-description as the prisoner of Jesus Christ, Ephesians 3:1.
Aramaic term rendered imprisonment — Ezra 7:26, the least of four penalties in the Persian decree.
Hebrews 13:3 gives the corresponding duty: remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them.
usage: “Bonds and imprisonment” — in the second half of Hebrews 11, where faith is not delivered.
“Of whom the world was not worthy” — said of the tortured, not the triumphant.
Half the New Testament epistles were written under guard.

pos: n. (the condition of a bondservant; used of Solomon's levy on Israel and of Judah's state in exile)
etymology: Latin servitudo, from servus, a slave. The Hebrew in 2 Chronicles 10:4 is abodah, service or labour; in Lamentations 1:3 it is the same root, describing the condition of a people carried away.
biblical_def: The word marks the moment the kingdom split. The northern tribes came to Rehoboam with a grievance: “Thy father made our yoke grievous: now therefore ease thou somewhat the grievous servitude of thy father, and his heavy yoke that he put upon us, and we will serve thee” (2 Chronicles 10:4). Solomon in his glory had laid a levy of forced labour on his own people, and the request is moderate — ease thou somewhat — and conditional loyalty is offered in return. Rehoboam refused on the counsel of the young men, and ten tribes were lost in a day. The second use describes what Judah came to: “Judah is gone into captivity because of affliction, and because of great servitude: she dwelleth among the heathen, she findeth no rest: all her persecutors overtook her between the straits” (Lamentations 1:3). What the nation imposed on itself under Solomon it endured from foreigners in exile. Between the two verses lies a long lesson about what a kingdom does with its own people, and Lamentations opens with the collapse of the city that was “princess among the provinces” (Lamentations 1:1) into tribute.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines servitude as the condition of a slave, the state of involuntary subjection to a master, and also service, or the state of a servant.
webster_full: SERVITUDE, n. The condition of a slave; the state of involuntary subjection to a master.
2. The state of a servant.
3. The office of a servant; service.
YOKE, n. Something that connects or binds; a chain; a link; a bond of connection.
2. A mark of servitude; slavery; bondage.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 10:4
Thy father made our yoke grievous: now therefore ease thou somewhat the grievous servitude of thy father, and his heavy yoke that he put upon us, and we will serve thee.
Lamentations 1:3
Judah is gone into captivity because of affliction, and because of great servitude: she dwelleth among the heathen, she findeth no rest: all her persecutors overtook her between the straits.
Lamentations 1:1
How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!
Ezra 7:26

And whosoever will not do the law of thy God, and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him, whether it be unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment.
corruption_summary: Solomon's levy is passed over because he is the wise king, and the text records it as the grievance that broke the kingdom.
corruption_paragraphs: Solomon is remembered for wisdom, wealth and the temple, and Scripture is candid about the bill. The forced labour that raised those buildings fell on his own people, and the first act of the next reign was a delegation asking for relief. The chronicler does not excuse it, and the division of the kingdom follows directly from Rehoboam's refusal to grant it. That is a hard word for any leader who has built something impressive on the backs of the people he was given to shepherd, and it is a hard word about legacy: the structures stood, and the kingdom did not. The prophets later make the same charge against rulers who build by unrighteousness and use their neighbour's service without wages.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the term. The principle to recover is the biblical treatment of bondage, which is neither the modern grievance framework nor a comfortable silence. Scripture regulates servitude sharply in the law — the seventh-year release, the prohibition of manstealing, the death penalty for it, and the requirement to send a freed servant away furnished — and the New Testament names menstealers among the lawless in 1 Timothy 1:10, a verse the abolitionists used with effect. It also commands masters to forbear threatening and to remember their own Master in heaven. Those are the categories: sin, oppression, restitution, and the fear of God, and they cut deeper than any analysis by group identity.
roots_summary: Hebrew abodah, labour or service — 2 Chronicles 10:4, Lamentations 1:3; ol, a yoke — 2 Chronicles 10:4; mas, a levy of forced labour — 1 Kings 5:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew abodah — labour, service, bondage; 2 Chronicles 10:4 and Lamentations 1:3.
Hebrew ol — a yoke; 2 Chronicles 10:4, the figure the northern tribes chose for Solomon's levy.
Hebrew mas — a levy, forced labour; 1 Kings 5:13, the institution behind the grievance.
Hebrew ebed — a servant or bondman; the common word, and the title of the Servant of Isaiah 53.
Exodus 21:16 sets the law against manstealing: he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, shall surely be put to death.
usage: “Ease thou somewhat the grievous servitude of thy father” — a moderate request, refused.
“Judah is gone into captivity… because of great servitude” — what she imposed, she endured.
The buildings stood; the kingdom did not.

pos: v. (commanded, laid upon with authority; used of the blood of the testament, of Purim, and of an apostolic authority Paul declines to use)
etymology: From Old French enjoindre, Latin injungere, to join on, to impose. To enjoin is to lay a thing upon someone as a charge — stronger than to advise, and in Scripture usually the act of one with the standing to require it.
biblical_def: The most weighty use is covenantal: Moses, having sprinkled the book and the people (Hebrews 9:19), spoke “This is the blood of the testament which God hath enjoined unto you” (Hebrews 9:20). The covenant is not an agreement negotiated between parties but a charge God enjoins, ratified in blood. Esther uses the word of the establishment of a memorial: the days of Purim were confirmed “according as Mordecai the Jew and Esther the queen had enjoined them, and as they had decreed for themselves and for their seed” (Esther 9:31). Job's friend Elihu uses it of God's freedom: “Who hath enjoined him his way? or who can say, Thou hast wrought iniquity?” (Job 36:23) — no one lays a charge on God. The most touching use is Paul's, writing to Philemon about a runaway slave: “Wherefore, though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee that which is convenient” (Philemon 1:8), and he does not enjoin. He appeals instead, for love's sake. The apostle who could have commanded chose to ask, and the whole letter turns on that decision.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines enjoin as to order or direct with urgency, to admonish or instruct with authority, and notes it implies authority in the one who enjoins.
webster_full: ENJOIN, v.t. To order or direct with urgency; to admonish or instruct with authority; to command.
2. Enjoin has the force of pressing admonition with authority; as, a parent enjoins on his children the duty of obedience.
3. In law, to forbid judicially; to issue an injunction against.
COMMAND, v.t. To bid; to order; to direct; to charge; implying authority, and power to control.
ENTREAT, v.t. To ask earnestly; to beseech; to petition or pray with urgency.
scriptures: Hebrews 9:20
Saying, This is the blood of the testament which God hath enjoined unto you.
Philemon 1:8
Wherefore, though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee that which is convenient,
Who hath enjoined him his way? or who can say, Thou hast wrought iniquity?
Esther 9:31

To confirm these days of Purim in their times appointed, according as Mordecai the Jew and Esther the queen had enjoined them, and as they had decreed for themselves and for their seed, the matters of the fastings and their cry.
corruption_summary: The covenant is reimagined as a contract between consenting parties, and the authority that enjoins it is negotiated away.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 9:20 says God enjoined the blood of the testament, and the verb settles a question modern theology likes to keep open. A covenant in Scripture is not a bargain struck between equals who each bring terms to the table; it is imposed by the greater on the lesser, and ratified in blood. Every framework that recasts the relation as a partnership between God and man, with man supplying his half, has lost the force of this verb. Job 36:23 puts the matter from the other direction: no one has enjoined God His way. He is under no charge laid by anyone, which is precisely why the charge He lays is absolute.

Philemon 1:8 is the necessary balance and it is a masterclass in the use of authority. Paul possessed apostolic power to command; he says so in the same sentence in which he declines to use it, choosing rather to beseech for love's sake, and calling himself Paul the aged and a prisoner of Jesus Christ. The corruption here runs in both directions. Some in authority enjoin everything, treating every preference as a charge to be laid on the conscience, which the regulative principle forbids. Others have so shrunk from authority that nothing is ever required at all. Paul shows the third way: real authority, consciously held, and voluntarily set aside in favour of appeal — which in that letter accomplished what a command could not.
roots_summary: Greek entellomai (G1781), to enjoin or charge — Hebrews 9:20; epitasso (G2004), to order — Philemon 8; Hebrew paqad and qiyyem — Esther 9:31, Job 36:23.
roots_lines: Greek entellomai (G1781) — to enjoin, to charge; Hebrews 9:20, of the blood of the testament.
Greek epitasso (G2004) — to order, to command with authority; Philemon 8, the authority Paul declines to use.
Greek parakaleo (G3870) — to beseech, to exhort alongside; Philemon 9, what he does instead.
Hebrew qum in the causative — to confirm, establish; Esther 9:31, of the days of Purim.
Philemon 9 gives the ground of the appeal: for love's sake I rather beseech thee, being such an one as Paul the aged.
usage: “The blood of the testament which God hath enjoined unto you” — imposed, not negotiated.
“Who hath enjoined him his way?” — no charge is laid upon God.
“Though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee” — and he beseeches instead.

pos: n. (the forehead; and the edge or projecting crest of a hill; both senses turned to account in Scripture)
etymology: Old English bru, the eyebrow or forehead. The Hebrew in Isaiah 48:4 is metsach, forehead; the Greek in Luke 4:29 is ophrus, an eyebrow, used of the overhanging edge of a hill.
biblical_def: Isaiah uses the word for hardness. The LORD names Israel's condition before He announces what He will do about it: “Because I knew that thou art obstinate, and thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass” (Isaiah 48:4). Three metaphors, all of unyielding material — and the point of the verse is that God knew this in advance and declared the former things beforehand precisely so that the nation could not credit its idols. The other sense is topographical and belongs to one of the most striking scenes in the Gospels. At Nazareth, after the Lord had read from Isaiah and applied it to Himself, the congregation “rose up, and thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong” (Luke 4:29). His own townsmen took Him to the edge of the cliff. And then: “But he passing through the midst of them went his way” (Luke 4:30). No struggle is described. Ezekiel supplies the redeemed use of the first sense: God tells His prophet, “I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads” (Ezekiel 3:8) — hardness given by God to withstand hardness bred by sin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brow as the prominent ridge over the eye, the forehead, and also the edge of a steep place.
webster_full: BROW, n. The prominent ridge over the eye, forming an arch above the orbit.
2. The forehead.
3. The general air of the countenance.
4. The edge of a steep place; as the brow of a hill.
BRAZEN, a. Made of brass; impudent; having a front like brass.
scriptures: Isaiah 48:4
Because I knew that thou art obstinate, and thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass;
Luke 4:29
And rose up, and thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong.
Luke 4:30
But he passing through the midst of them went his way,
Ezekiel 3:8
Behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads.
corruption_summary: Hardness is treated as a fixed temperament or as a virtue in itself, when Scripture distinguishes sharply between the brow God hardens and the brow sin has made brass.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 48:4 and Ezekiel 3:8 use nearly the same image for opposite things. Israel's brow is brass because she will not hear; the prophet's forehead is made strong by God so that he can go on speaking to her. The difference is not in the hardness but in its source and its direction. A man may mistake mere stubbornness for prophetic courage, and Scripture supplies the test: God gave Ezekiel a hard forehead to bear rejection, not to deliver it. Firmness that only ever costs other people something, and never the man himself, has more in common with Isaiah's brass than with Ezekiel's commission.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what happened at the brow of the hill in Nazareth. His neighbours — men who had watched Him grow up — took Him to a cliff edge because He told them the truth about themselves from their own Scriptures, and He walked through the middle of them. The sovereignty of that moment is easily missed: the crowd did not relent, and He was not rescued by anyone. His hour was not yet come, and no mob on any hillside could advance it by a day. The same is true of every servant of His who has ever been thrust out of a city.
roots_summary: Hebrew metsach, forehead — Isaiah 48:4, Ezekiel 3:8; Greek ophrus (G3790), a brow or edge — Luke 4:29, its only occurrence.
roots_lines: Hebrew metsach — forehead, brow; Isaiah 48:4 of brass, and Ezekiel 3:8-9 of the prophet's strengthened forehead.
Greek ophrus (G3790) — an eyebrow, hence the overhanging brow of a hill; Luke 4:29, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Hebrew qasheh — hard, obstinate; Isaiah 48:4, with the iron sinew of the neck.
Hebrew shamir — adamant, the hardest stone; Ezekiel 3:9, harder than flint have I made thy forehead.
Luke 4:30 records the outcome without explanation: he passing through the midst of them went his way.
usage: “Thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass” — hardness bred by sin.
“I have made thy forehead strong against their foreheads” — hardness given to bear rejection.
“Unto the brow of the hill… But he passing through the midst of them went his way”.
